I'll solve this directly. The problem asks for a group $G$ such that the natural homomorphism $\varphi: G \to \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ (conjugation) is an isomorphism. I'll use $G = S_3$.

---

**Claim.** $G = S_3$ satisfies the requirement: the map $\varphi: S_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}(S_3)$, $g \mapsto f_g$ (conjugation by $g$), is an isomorphism.

**Proof.**

The map $\varphi$ is always a homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ with $\ker\varphi = Z(G)$, the center. So $\varphi$ is an isomorphism iff (i) $Z(G)=\{e\}$ (injectivity) and (ii) every automorphism is inner, i.e. $\mathrm{Inn}(G)=\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ (surjectivity). We verify both for $S_3$.

**Step 1: $Z(S_3)=\{e\}$ (injectivity).**

The elements of $S_3$ are $e$, the three transpositions $(12),(13),(23)$, and the two $3$-cycles $(123),(132)$. Conjugation sends $(12)\mapsto(13)$ via $(23)(12)(23)=(13)$, so transpositions are not central. Also $(123)\mapsto(132)$ via $(12)(123)(12)=(132)$, so $3$-cycles are not central. Hence no non-identity element commutes with everything, giving $Z(S_3)=\{e\}$. Thus $\varphi$ is injective.

**Step 2: $\mathrm{Aut}(S_3)=\mathrm{Inn}(S_3)$ (surjectivity).**

Let $\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut}(S_3)$. Automorphisms preserve element order, so $\alpha$ permutes the set $T=\{(12),(13),(23)\}$ of elements of order $2$ and the set $C=\{(123),(132)\}$ of elements of order $3$. Since any two distinct transpositions generate $S_3$ (e.g. $(12),(13)$ generate it), the automorphism $\alpha$ is completely determined by its action on $T$.

Now consider the conjugation action of $S_3$ on $T$. Conjugation by $(23)$ sends $(12)\mapsto(13)$, and conjugation by $(13)$ sends $(12)\mapsto(23)$. So the orbit of $(12)$ under conjugation is all of $T$, and the stabilizer of $(12)$ is $\{e,(12)\}$, giving $|\text{orbit}|=|S_3|/2=3=|T|$. Hence $S_3$ acts transitively on $T$. The induced homomorphism $\psi:S_3\to\mathrm{Sym}(T)\cong S_3$ has kernel $Z(S_3)=\{e\}$, so $\psi$ is injective, hence bijective. Therefore **every** permutation of $T$ is realized by some inner automorphism $\iota_g$.

In particular, for our arbitrary $\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut}(S_3)$, there exists $g\in S_3$ such that $\iota_g$ and $\alpha$ agree on $T$. Since $T$ generates $S_3$, we have $\alpha=\iota_g=\varphi(g)$. Hence $\alpha$ is inner, so $\mathrm{Aut}(S_3)=\mathrm{Inn}(S_3)=\varphi(S_3)$.

**Conclusion.** $\varphi:S_3\to\mathrm{Aut}(S_3)$ is injective (Step 1) and surjective (Step 2), hence an isomorphism. $\blacksquare$
